text: What shape should upkeep take?
context: Today armies cost nothing to keep. The South earns no Manpower at the start, so any upkeep needs an allowance or it goes broke in its first turns.

options.label: A. Each unit costs Manpower every turn by its full size (half a point per 1,000 men); each side's depots feed the first 6
options.rationale: Militia pays 1.25 a turn and an infantry regiment 0.35, with no special rule. At the start only the Republic pays: 5 to 7 of its 27, depending on the size of security forces.

options.label: B. Every army costs 1 Manpower a turn
options.rationale: Simplest, but the South is broke at the end of turn 1 and a truck column costs as much as a militia column.

options.label: C. Option A, plus half a Fund a turn for each gun, tank, truck and aircraft
options.rationale: More realistic, and one more number to read.

options.label: D. A supply limit: each whole territory feeds three armies, each one over costs 1 Manpower
options.rationale: Easy to see, but losing ground raises the bill at once.

text: What happens when a side can't feed its armies?
context: It should hurt without ending the game. Units cost less to feed as they lose men, so the bill shrinks.

options.label: A. No recruiting or Replenish, and the missing Manpower leaves as men, at most 10% of a unit a turn and never below half
options.rationale: No unit is ever lost to hunger, and it needs no new order.

options.label: B. No recruiting or Replenish, and nothing else
options.rationale: Gentlest; a side can sit on a large unpaid army.

options.label: C. Let players disband units
options.rationale: More control, but a new order the computer player must learn too.

text: Which value package should we build?
context: Both make armies cost something to keep, builds pay back sooner and regulars cheaper. Moderate passes 11 of 12 economy tests, Bold 10 and today 2. The tests were used to tune Moderate, so a pass isn't proof of balance.

options.label: A. Moderate
options.rationale: The same units, prices and incomes you know, moved. By arithmetic, a Republic raising only militia reaches 91 attack on turn 10 instead of 318.

options.label: B. Bold: twice the upkeep, plus Funds upkeep for machines
options.rationale: Makes Manpower a real limit for everyone, but a large Republican army outgrows its income.

options.label: C. Upkeep only; leave prices and builds alone
options.rationale: Smallest change. Mines still pay back on turn 10, and the North's militia still adds 77 percent more attack than its regulars.

text: How should militia change?
context: Today it has the most attack and defence for its price and trains fastest. It holds and storms equally well.

options.label: A. 3 Funds (from 2), attack 2 (from 3), defence stays 4
options.rationale: Militia holds ground, regulars take it: militia alone adds less attack than regulars for every side (the North is closest, at 92 percent). The Republic loses 5 of its 64 starting attack.

options.label: B. 3 Funds, attack and defence unchanged
options.rationale: Easier to accept, but the North's militia still adds 38 percent more attack than its regulars.

options.label: C. 4 Funds, values unchanged
options.rationale: Militia becomes an emergency buy, and the North's still adds 4 percent more attack than its regulars.

text: What should security forces be for?
context: Infantry beats them on every number at the same price, as you noticed.

options.label: A. A quick garrison: 4 Funds, 1 Manpower, 1,000 men, trained in 1 turn
options.rationale: Cheaper and faster than infantry, and weaker.

options.label: B. Keep the price and make them 4/6, like infantry
options.rationale: Then they duplicate infantry.

options.label: C. A city specialist: a bonus when defending a city
options.rationale: More flavour, but a new kind of unit effect.

text: How fast should mines and industry pay back?
context: A mine started on turn 1 pays back on turn 10 and Industry on turn 13. Past simulations ended at a median of 12 to 15 turns; your games end before turn 10.

options.label: A. Cheaper and 2 turns to build: mines back by turn 6, industry by turn 7
options.rationale: A turn-3 build still profits in a 10-turn game. Building in a month is quicker than history.

options.label: B. Keep the build times and cut prices further
options.rationale: Truer to history, and the first payment still comes late.

options.label: C. Make each industry level pay 2
options.rationale: Doubles the industry already standing: the Republic gains 10 Funds a turn at once.

text: Should some building cost Manpower as well as Funds?
context: The North has 27 Manpower a turn but only 5 Funds, so it can't spend its men. No number in either package fixes that without touching incomes.

options.label: A. Yes: fortifications, roads and rail take part of their price in Manpower
options.rationale: Labour battalions did this work, and men become useful to a poor side.

options.label: B. No, but give the North more Funds
options.rationale: Simple, and it makes the strongest computer side stronger.

options.label: C. No, but trim the farms
options.rationale: Less Manpower for everyone; you said the incomes feel right.

text: When Popular Resistance goes, what should replace it?
context: It takes 3 off the attacker's die in Republican cities, worth 15 points of success chance in a contested city fight. Past simulations gave the Republic 10 to 16 percent of wins even with it, so removing it and adding upkeep both hurt the Republic.

options.label: A. Barricades worth 2 in any city, for every side
options.rationale: Gives back 5 of the 15 points evenly, and city fighting stays hard for all.

options.label: B. Nothing
options.rationale: Cleanest; expect the Republic to win less.

options.label: C. Barricades worth 2, and Madrid and Barcelona start fortified
options.rationale: Gives those two capitals 10 more points.

options.label: D. Barricades worth 2, and 10 more starting Funds for the Republic
options.rationale: Two more regiments from the Bank of Spain's reserves.

text: When a rival is one step from winning, what should the computer players do?
context: Today a rival one step short makes them value guarding their own ground more (4 times) than attacking the leader's (2.5 times), and the last army on such ground never leaves. They see a human leader as well as a computer one.

options.label: A. Attack the leader as readily as they guard, accept worse odds, and count a foothold that spoils a territory as a full success
options.rationale: One foothold takes a territory off the leader's count, which is the cheapest way to stop a win.

options.label: B. Attack the leader only, and stop guarding
options.rationale: Aggressive, but an easily led army leaves its own ground open.

options.label: C. Keep the present balance and only fix what it overlooks: a leader needing a third side's ground, or two territories at once
options.rationale: Smaller change, but still defensive.

text: Should the computer players change how they spend when a rival is close to winning?
context: Today their recruiting and building ignore it. They set aside 30 percent of Funds for builds.

options.label: A. Yes: at 2 steps or fewer, no saving for builds, and prefer units that train in one turn
options.rationale: New units arrive in time to matter.

options.label: B. Yes, but only at one step
options.rationale: Later, and often too late for a 2-turn unit.

options.label: C. No
options.rationale: Keeps the economy steady, at the cost of losing the game first.

text: How should the music be delivered?
context: One 16 MB file is downloaded whole within seconds by Firefox and Safari on a fast connection, even if the player leaves after a minute. Chrome takes about 6 MB.

options.label: Four files, one per track, with the fades built in
options.rationale: A first listen costs 1.4 to 3.4 MB, a session can start on a different track, and no fading script is needed on iPhone. Needs a small change to the mix script.

options.label: One file, the mix as it is
options.rationale: Simplest and exactly your mix, but 6 to 16 MB on a first listen and it always opens the same way.

options.label: Music only as a download the player asks for
options.rationale: Cheapest, but most players would never hear it.

text: Which quality should the music ship at?
context: All four tracks: Opus 64 is 10.8 MB, Opus 96 is 16.3 MB. iPhones use a separate AAC copy (16.2 MB at 96). Listen to the samples above in headphones first.

options.label: Opus 64 and AAC 96, after you listen
options.rationale: A third smaller. Best if you cannot tell the difference in headphones; please compare on Unraveling.

options.label: Opus 96 and AAC 96
options.rationale: Closer to the usual guideline, 5.5 MB more in total.

options.label: Opus 96 and AAC 128
options.rationale: Nearest to your current files, 16 to 21 MB.

text: What should happen with sound on a first visit?
context: Browsers do not allow sound before a click.

options.label: Music starts with the first campaign, at a modest level, with a notice and a mute button
options.rationale: Players hear it, and one press stops it.

options.label: Everything starts off until the player turns it on
options.rationale: Never annoys, but most players will not find it.

options.label: Effects on, music off
options.rationale: A middle path that hides the music.

text: Which sounds should we make now?
context: Fourteen candidates are in the audition board. Every licence was checked; none has been listened to by us.

options.label: Your eight, plus a soft refused tick and one distant-guns sound when the battle report opens
options.rationale: Covers your list and gives the report some weight, about 0.1 MB in all.

options.label: Only your eight
options.rationale: Fewest sounds to tire of.

options.label: Your eight plus victory, defeat and weather
options.rationale: More atmosphere, and more to license and tune.

text: Which candidate sounds do you like? Tick every one to keep.
context: Play them in the board above. The ticks for the recommended set are a starting guess: no one on the research team could listen. Leave out anything that sounds wrong and I'll find another.

options.label: Create order: Typewriter burst
Create order: Marker set down
Recruit: Snare drum roll
Recruit: Rubber stamp
Build: Two anvil strikes
Air mission: Fighter flyover
Air mission: Twin-propeller flyover
Rail move: Whistle, then train on rails
Truck move: Diesel pulls away
Reinforce on foot: Squad marching
End turn: Orchestral hit with horns
End turn: Two drum strikes (made for this game)
Battle report opens: Distant cannon
Order refused: Soft double tick

text: How strict should the limits on repeated sounds be?
context: Ten rail orders at once would be ten whistles and about 5 dB over the maximum, which crackles. Try both in the mix lab.

options.label: Strict: one sound per action, a special sound at most every four seconds, then a quiet tick
options.rationale: Special sounds stay special. Four seconds is a starting value to tune by ear.

options.label: Looser: special sounds every second or so
options.rationale: Livelier, and tires faster.

options.label: Special sounds only for the first order of each kind each turn
options.rationale: Calmest, and the player may wonder why a later train is silent.

text: When should the detailed map picture load?
context: It is 1.8 MB of the 3.1 MB a new player downloads, and it loads before anyone zooms in.

options.label: Only when the player zooms in, or when idle on a fast connection
options.rationale: Cuts up to 59% for players who do not zoom. A zoom may be soft for a moment.

options.label: As now, at the start of the campaign
options.rationale: Sharp at once, and the largest cost in the game.

options.label: On zoom, and re-encode it smaller
options.rationale: A further 0.8 MB or so in all, but the map must be looked at and the visual tests refreshed.

text: Should a download size limit stop a build?
context: A limit exists and is already missed (159.4 kB against 155 kB for the first script), but nothing runs the check.

options.label: Yes, after moving the rules and computer player out of the first script, and cover audio and images too
options.rationale: Keeps growth visible, and the limit stays where you set it.

options.label: Yes, from today, blocking
options.rationale: Nothing else can merge until the miss is fixed.

options.label: Report only
options.rationale: Easy, and easily ignored, as now.

text: What should an aircraft card print?
context: Aircraft attack and defence are 0 and 1 for every type, so they say nothing.

options.label: The role (FTR, BOMB, RCN), with the bonus at the closest zoom
options.rationale: Says what the squadron is for.

options.label: Attack-defence like other units
options.rationale: Consistent, but always 0-1.

options.label: Symbol only
options.rationale: Clean, but less information.

text: How should Recruit show a unit's special effects?
context: The list shows none of them today.

options.label: Small chips under the price, tap for the detail
options.rationale: Visible on a phone and wraps in a narrow pane.

options.label: A fold-out line per unit
options.rationale: Shorter rows, hidden until opened.

options.label: A comparison table
options.rationale: Useful later; too wide for a narrow pane.

text: Should the battle sheet show why a unit's strength is what it is (men, morale), not just the total?
context: The game does not record this per unit today, so showing it needs a small change to what each battle saves.

options.label: Yes, show men and morale per unit
options.rationale: Players can see why a unit counted for less; small engine change.

options.label: No, total strength only
options.rationale: No engine change, but less explanation.

text: On Invade, keep the odds pinned while you scroll the units?
context: Today the pinned box fills the pane. You asked for the details at the top; a thin one-line odds bar could stay.

options.label: Keep a one-line odds bar, scroll the defenders away
options.rationale: Shows 4 units instead of 0, and the odds stay in view.

options.label: Scroll everything
options.rationale: Most room once scrolled; only 2 units at the top.

options.label: Two tabs: Your units and Defenders
options.rationale: Same room as the first, one more tap.

text: What should the casualty counter count?
context: The game records battle losses and frostbite. Units that surrender or are disbanded don't record their men yet.

options.label: All men lost: battles, surrenders, disbanded units and cold
options.rationale: Matches what players expect from casualties; needs men added to surrender records.

options.label: Battle losses only
options.rationale: Simplest, but a surrendered army counts as no loss.

options.label: Battle losses and surrenders only
options.rationale: Leaves out cold losses, which are small.

text: Where should the casualty total sit, and how long can it be?
context: The top bar already overflows at 1280 px. At 1440 the long form does not fit beside the name.

options.label: Beside the faction name, as 12.4k, tapping shows the split by side
options.rationale: Fits and is nearest the turn counter.

options.label: In full in the turn row, replacing the readiness chips when narrow
options.rationale: Closest, but crowds the row.

options.label: In the menu
options.rationale: No room problem, harder to see.

text: The game no longer uses the old six-sided-die battle rules, but most tests still run on them. Remove them?
context: About 1,000 lines of code and many tests pin the map to the old rules. Removing them simplifies the code, but a future era could use them.

options.label: Keep the old rules for now, and move the tests that should follow the real game to the current dice
options.rationale: Tests then check what players play; deleting code can follow later.

options.label: Remove them completely
options.rationale: Simplest code, most test work, and no old-rules option for other eras.

options.label: Leave everything as it is
options.rationale: No cost, but the cruft and wrong-rules tests remain.

text: When should the pruning happen?
context: The safe removals are small and touch many files, so they collide with feature work if both run at once.

options.label: Safe removals first, before the feature work starts
options.rationale: Everyone builds on the smaller code, and the unused-code check then stops regrowth.

options.label: A pass at the end
options.rationale: Also catches what Rev 3 leaves behind, but merges are harder.

options.label: Both
options.rationale: Cleanest result, and about twice the pruning cost.

text: Should a paved airfield still let aircraft fly in rain and snow?
context: Open since Rev 2. You chose "rain and snow ground all air", but the building has no other use.

options.label: Yes, keep the exception
options.rationale: Gives the upgrade a purpose, and it costs only 4 Funds in the Moderate package.

options.label: No: ground everything and remove the building
options.rationale: Simpler, and one more thing pruned.

text: Should trucks move on any road, not only main roads?
context: Open since Rev 2. On the opening map only Madrid to Valencia is main road all the way, and the Republic has no trucks. You also asked for a truck sound, which would almost never play.

options.label: Yes, any road, but still not across a mountain pass
options.rationale: Trucks become worth buying at the new price.

options.label: No, leave it rare
options.rationale: Truer to 1936; trucks stay a niche.

text: May I run balance sims on the finished economy?
context: Nothing here predicts win rates. A 400-game run would take roughly half an hour of this Mac's time (estimated from the 10-game unit test) and few tokens. Sims only show computer against computer, so they can't prove that a person's militia spam is beaten; your playtest does that.

options.label: Yes: one run on the finished build, and one more after a single correction
options.rationale: Removing Popular Resistance and adding upkeep both push the Republic down from 10 to 16 percent of wins, by an unknown amount.

options.label: Only after I've playtested
options.rationale: Your feel first, numbers second.

options.label: No sims in Rev 3
options.rationale: Playtests and the tenet checks only.
